To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

technological convergence is the dominant driver of labor productivity growth in manufacturing, and that the process of technological convergence is driven primarily by OECD countries and is largely independent from growth determinants.

1) technological growth at the global level is driven primarily the US and a small number of other countries 2) there is evidence of strong convergence in both technology, and capital labor ratios and 3) very few of the standard growth determinants are shown to enhance the process catching up in technology.

i) technological growth is a major determinant of labor productivity growth, ii) technological growth is driven primarily by a handful of countries (the US, Germany, Japan), and iii) there is strong evidence of technological convergence.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether the process of convergence in labor productivity growth that we observe in the manufacturing sector is due to convergence across countries in the level of capital labor ratios, technological productivity and total factor productivity.
the decomposition of labor productivity into the contributions of technological change, capital accumulation, and total factor productivity growth.

the following questions: How much of the growth of labor productivity is driven by technological progress versus capital accumulation? How does the contribution of technology vary across countries, sectors and over time? Is there convergence in technology across countries? What are the determinants of convergence in technology?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the process of convergence is mainly driven by capital accumulation, but that technological convergence is not negligible.
technology is the main driver of convergence, but that capital accumulation plays a non negligible role in explaining convergence in labor productivity growth.
technology is the main driver of convergence in manufacturing labor productivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
technological catching up is driven primarily by convergence in capital labor ratio.
technology matters a lot and that it is not the usual suspects that drive technological catching up.
the convergence in technology is a much more powerful force than the one in capital accumulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
convergence in TEP has been a key driver of labor productivity growth in manufacturing, and that this process is driven by a large set of developing countries.
convergence in technology and capital accumulation are two key factors behind the convergence in labor productivities observed in manufacturing.
the process of convergence in manufacturing is primarily driven by the diffusion of capital, and not by the diffusion of technology.
